review.note: Original content following 4HI1 Historical investigation A4, key topic 2.

learn.intro: After Geneva, the USA backed a non-communist South Vietnam to stop the 'dominoes' falling. But Diem's government was unpopular, the NLF grew, and by 1964 the USA was on the edge of full-scale war.

sections.title: 1. Geneva, the domino theory and the formation of South Vietnam

blocks.p: The Geneva Conference (1954) aimed to end the war and divide Vietnam temporarily, with elections in 1956. The USA did not sign the agreement; it feared Ho Chi Minh would win any election.

President Eisenhower explained US policy with the domino theory (1954): if one country fell to communism, its neighbours would follow, like a row of dominoes. The USA set up SEATO (1954) and supported a separate state in the South.
Ngo Dinh Diem became leader of South Vietnam (the Republic of Vietnam) after a rigged referendum in 1955. With US support he refused to hold the 1956 elections.

sections.title: 2. Life in North and South Vietnam

blocks.p: North (Ho Chi Minh): a communist state. Land reform (1953–56) took land from landlords and gave it to peasants, but it was carried out brutally and thousands were killed; Ho later admitted mistakes. Industry and farming were brought under state control.

South (Ngo Dinh Diem): Diem was a Catholic in a mainly Buddhist country and favoured Catholics and his own family; his brother Nhu ran the secret police. Land reform helped landlords more than peasants. Opponents were imprisoned and corruption was widespread, so the government lost support in the countryside.

evidence: 1953–56: brutal land reform in the North.
Diem favoured Catholics; his brother Nhu ran the secret police.

sections.title: 3. Ho's policies to unite Vietnam: the NLF and the Ho Chi Minh Trail

blocks.p: Ho was determined to unite Vietnam. In December 1960 the National Liberation Front (NLF) was set up in the South, with Northern backing, to overthrow Diem. Its fighters were called the Vietcong by their enemies. They used guerrilla tactics and won peasant support by redistributing land, though they also used terror against officials.
The Ho Chi Minh Trail — a network of paths through Laos and Cambodia — carried soldiers and supplies from North to South. It was very hard to cut because it ran through jungle and neutral countries.

evidence: The Ho Chi Minh Trail ran through Laos and Cambodia.

sections.title: 4. The US response, the fall of Diem and the Gulf of Tonkin

blocks.p: The USA sent money, weapons and military advisers. Under President Kennedy the number of advisers rose from under 1,000 in 1961 to about 16,000 by 1963.

The Strategic Hamlet Programme (1962) moved peasants into fortified villages to cut them off from the Vietcong. Peasants resented being moved from their land and ancestral graves; many hamlets were badly built and infiltrated, and the programme increased support for the NLF.

In 1963 Buddhist protests grew; the monk Thich Quang Duc burned himself to death in Saigon in June, and the photographs shocked the world. With US approval, South Vietnamese generals overthrew Diem in November 1963; he and Nhu were killed. Unstable military governments followed.

In August 1964 the US destroyer Maddox reported attacks by North Vietnamese boats in the Gulf of Tonkin (the second attack probably did not happen). Congress passed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, allowing President Johnson to take 'all necessary measures' — a blank cheque for war.

He favoured Catholics and his family and repressed opponents

options: Peasants resented being moved and many hamlets were infiltrated
mcq.why: It increased support for the NLF.

mcq.q: What did the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution allow?
options: The President to take 'all necessary measures'

matching.title: Match the President to the policy

evidence.q: Give precise evidence that US involvement increased under Kennedy.
evidence.model: US advisers rose from under 1,000 in 1961 to about 16,000 by 1963, and the USA backed the Strategic Hamlet Programme (1962).

flashcards.q: Why did the USA not sign the Geneva Agreements?
flashcards.a: It feared Ho Chi Minh would win the 1956 elections and Vietnam would become communist.

flashcards.q: What was life like in North Vietnam?
flashcards.a: Communist state; brutal land reform (1953–56) took land from landlords; state control of industry.

flashcards.q: How did the NLF win support?
flashcards.a: Redistributing land, guerrilla tactics, anger at Diem — but also terror against officials.

flashcards.q: Why did the USA allow Diem's overthrow?
flashcards.a: His repression of Buddhists and unpopularity were undermining the war against the NLF.

flashcards.q: Why was the Gulf of Tonkin incident significant?
flashcards.a: It led to the Resolution giving Johnson power to escalate the war without a declaration of war.

checklist.text: I can explain the aims of Geneva, the US response and the domino theory.
I can describe life in North and South Vietnam under Ho and Diem.
I can explain the impact of the NLF and the Ho Chi Minh Trail.
I can judge how far US involvement increased under Kennedy and Johnson to 1964.
